newsitem.title: JAPAN: Big Bang may be whimper for Tokyo bourse - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Big Bang may be whimper for Tokyo bourse - analysts.

text.p: "Big Bang" financial reforms planned by Japan should give Tokyo stock market a new lease of life, analysts say, but may not be enough to turn around its slumping foreign section.

Market participants said they welcome the deregulation trend, but wonder if the government will take the further steps they say are needed to transform the stock exchange into an open and less costly market comparable with overseas centres.

"I think the overall (reform) trend is heading in the right direction, but the point is, can Japan really reach the same level as Hong Kong and the United States soon?" said a senior foreign broker at a "Big Four" securities house.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto last month unveiled a five-year Big Bang plan to liberalise Japan's financial markets and try to catch up with reforms carried out more than a decade ago in Europe and North America.
Although German telecoms giant Deutsche Telekom successfully listed in Tokyo last month, steep listing costs and red tape have been driving other foreign firms away.

There are now just 68 foreign firms listed in Tokyo, down from a peak of 125 in 1991, just after Japan's "bubble economy" of inflated asset prices burst. Deutsche Telekom was the first listing by a U.S. or European firm in Tokyo since 1993.
The drop is even more drastic when compared with other bourses. From 1991 to 1995, the number of foreign listings in New York more than doubled to 247 firms.
And although there was also a fall in London to 531 firms from 604, the decline was much less severe than in Tokyo.
Trading volume in foreign stocks in Tokyo has also plunged, totalling just under 40 million shares last year, down from 755 million shares in 1987, according to exchange data.

A special committee of an advisory panel to the finance minister unveiled a list of 22 items last week it may propose in an effort to help Hashimoto's reforms succeed and make Japan's securities markets more attractive.
But the proposals focus on liberalisation of stock broking commission fees and abolishing the walls between securities houses and insurance firms.
Analysts said that while the reforms will help the market, they are unlikely attract foreign firms.

"Financial authorities must be well aware of the problems in Tokyo," said the senior foreign stock broker, adding that the regulations and costs involved in maintaining a Tokyo listing would not change.
Companies must meet stringent capital and turnover requirements before they can list in Tokyo, and also face heavy annual fees and considerable paperwork.

Although costs of being listed vary according to the number of shares issued, a Japanese blue-chip company said recent figures show basic annual payments of 14.55 million yen ($128,000) in Tokyo, $10,800 in London and $16,170 in New York.
But some underwriters said that after the successful listing of Deutsche Telekom, it was likely to be followed by other telecoms firms next year.

Shinichi Ichikawa, a strategist at the research department of Credit Lyonnais Securities (Japan), said telecoms firms wanted to list in Japan to raise their profiles amid increased worldwide competition.

"They need to make their names well-known in Japan, as the potential in the telecommunications market here is huge," he said. "But listing in Tokyo is not always seen as effective for other companies."
